Main article: [List of medieval universities](/wiki/List_of_medieval_universities "List of medieval universities")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Mediaeval_universities.jpg/500px-Mediaeval_universities.jpg)](/wiki/File:Mediaeval_universities.jpg)

A 1911 map of [medieval universities](/wiki/Medieval_university "Medieval university") in Europe

This list includes [medieval universities](/wiki/Medieval_universities "Medieval universities") that were founded before 1500 and which have retained institutional continuity since then (excluding not only those that ceased to exist, but also those that merged into or split away to an institution which is regarded as newly established). Several of these have been closed for brief periods: for example the [University of Siena](/wiki/University_of_Siena "University of Siena") was closed 1805–1815 during [the Napoleonic Wars](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy_(Napoleonic) "Kingdom of Italy (Napoleonic)"), and universities in the [Czech Republic](/wiki/Czech_Republic "Czech Republic") and [Poland](/wiki/Poland "Poland") were closed during [Nazi occupation](/wiki/German-occupied_Europe "German-occupied Europe"), 1938–1945.

Universities are dated from when, according to scholars, they first met the definition of a university. In cases such as the universities of [Bologna](/wiki/University_of_Bologna "University of Bologna") and [Oxford](/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") which trace their history back to teaching in individual schools prior to their formation into a university, or which existed in another form prior to being a university, the date in the list below is thus later than the date given by the institutions for their foundation.[[18]](#cite_note-21)

The [Platonic solids](/wiki/Platonic_solid "Platonic solid") are five polyhedra known since antiquity. The set is named for [Plato](/wiki/Plato "Plato"), who attributed these solids to nature in his dialogue [*Timaeus*](/wiki/Timaeus_(dialogue) "Timaeus (dialogue)"). One of them, the cube, represented the [classical element](/wiki/Classical_element "Classical element") of [earth](/wiki/Earth_(classical_element) "Earth (classical element)") because of the building blocks of Earth's foundation.[[52]](#cite_note-djkt-52) [Euclid](/wiki/Euclid "Euclid")'s [*Elements*](/wiki/Euclid%27s_Elements "Euclid's Elements") defined the Platonic solids, including the cube, and showed how to find the ratio of the circumscribed sphere's diameter to the edge length.[[53]](#cite_note-heath-53)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Emmanuel_College_Front_Court%2C_Cambridge%2C_UK_-_Diliff.jpg/250px-Emmanuel_College_Front_Court%2C_Cambridge%2C_UK_-_Diliff.jpg)](/wiki/File:Emmanuel_College_Front_Court,_Cambridge,_UK_-_Diliff.jpg)

The [31 colleges](/wiki/Colleges_of_the_University_of_Cambridge "Colleges of the University of Cambridge") of the present-day University of Cambridge were originally an incidental feature of the university; no college within the University of Cambridge is as old as the university itself. The colleges within the university were initially endowed fellowships of scholars. There were also institutions without endowments, called hostels, which were gradually absorbed by the colleges over the centuries, and they have left some traces, including the naming of Garret Hostel Lane and [Garret Hostel Bridge](/wiki/Garret_Hostel_Bridge "Garret Hostel Bridge"), a street and bridge in Cambridge.[[24]](#cite_note-25)

The University of Cambridge's first college, [Peterhouse](/wiki/Peterhouse,_Cambridge "Peterhouse, Cambridge"), was founded in 1284 by [Hugh de Balsham](/wiki/Hugh_de_Balsham "Hugh de Balsham"), the [Bishop of Ely](/wiki/Bishop_of_Ely "Bishop of Ely"). The **Grammy Award for Best Alternative Music Performance** is an award presented by the [Recording Academy](/wiki/The_Recording_Academy "The Recording Academy") to honor quality [alternative music](/wiki/Alternative_Music "Alternative Music") performances in any given year. The award was presented for the first time on February 5, 2023, at the [65th Annual Grammy Awards](/wiki/65th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "65th Annual Grammy Awards"). It is a companion category to the [Grammy Award for Best Alternative Music Album](/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Alternative_Music_Album "Grammy Award for Best Alternative Music Album") and the first new category in the alternative genre field since the field's creation in 1991.

The **World Marathon Majors** (**WMM**) is a championship-style competition for [marathon](/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") runners that started in 2006. A points-based competition founded on seven major marathon races recognised as the most high-profile on the calendar, the series comprises annual races (in order of their founding) for the cities of [Boston](/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon") (1897), [New York](/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon") (1970), [Berlin](/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") (1974), [Chicago](/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") (1977), [London](/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") (1981), [Sydney](/wiki/Sydney_Marathon "Sydney Marathon") (2000), and [Tokyo](/wiki/Tokyo_Marathon "Tokyo Marathon") (2007).

In addition, the **World Marathon Majors** includes the results of any major global championship marathon held in that year. These races are the biennial [World Athletics Championships](/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") Marathon, and the quadrennial [Olympic Games](/wiki/Athletics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the Summer Olympics") Marathon.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Earth is [rounded](/wiki/Hydrostatic_equilibrium "Hydrostatic equilibrium") into [an ellipsoid](/wiki/Earth_ellipsoid "Earth ellipsoid") with [a circumference](/wiki/Earth%27s_circumference "Earth's circumference") of about 40,000 kilometers (24,900 miles). It is the [densest planet in the Solar System](/wiki/List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size "List of Solar System objects by size"). Of the four [rocky planets](/wiki/Rocky_planets "Rocky planets"), it is the largest and most massive. Earth is about eight [light-minutes](/wiki/Light-minute "Light-minute") (1 [AU](/wiki/Astronomical_Unit "Astronomical Unit")) away from the Sun and [orbits it](/wiki/Earth%27s_orbit "Earth's orbit"), taking a year (about 365.25 days) to complete one revolution. [Earth rotates](/wiki/Earth%27s_rotation "Earth's rotation") around its own axis in slightly less than a day (in about 23 hours and 56 minutes). [Earth's axis of rotation](#Axial_tilt_and_seasons) is tilted with respect to the perpendicular to its orbital plane around the Sun, producing seasons. Earth is [orbited](/wiki/Orbit "Orbit") by one permanent [natural satellite](/wiki/Natural_satellite "Natural satellite"), the [Moon](/wiki/Moon "Moon"), which orbits Earth at 384,400 km (238,855 mi)—1.28 light seconds—and is roughly a quarter as wide as Earth. The Moon's gravity helps stabilize Earth's axis, causes [tides](/wiki/Tide "Tide") and [gradually slows Earth's rotation](/wiki/Tidal_acceleration "Tidal acceleration"). Likewise, Earth's gravitational pull has already made the Moon's rotation [tidally locked](/wiki/Tidally_locked "Tidally locked"), keeping the same [near side](/wiki/Near_side_of_the_Moon "Near side of the Moon") facing Earth.

Earth, like most other bodies in the Solar System, [formed about 4.5 billion years ago](/wiki/Age_of_Earth "Age of Earth") from gas and dust in the [early Solar System](/wiki/Formation_and_evolution_of_the_Solar_System "Formation and evolution of the Solar Sy

Hall completed a combined arts and architecture degree at [Sydney University](/wiki/University_of_Sydney "University of Sydney"). Upon graduation a travel scholarship enabled him to spend twelve months in Europe during which time he visited Utzon in [Hellebæk](/wiki/Helleb%C3%A6k "Hellebæk").[[76]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-76) Returning to Sydney, Hall worked for the Government Architect, a branch of the NSW Public Works Department. While there he established himself as a talented design architect with a number of court and university buildings, including the Goldstein Hall at the University of New South Wales, which won the [Sir John Sulman Medal](/wiki/Sir_John_Sulman_Medal "Sir John Sulman Medal") in 1964.

Millken served as the 12th chancellor of the University of Texas System from September 2018 to May 2025. When he was announced as chancellor, the University of Texas System Board of Regents touted Milliken's rich higher education experience over three decades and his track record of success in creating and executing strategic plans.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

In a radio interview with KUT in October, 2022, Milliken announced that the UT System had exceeded enrollment of 244,000 students, system-wide, for the first time in history. Milliken credited the system's enrollment growth to improved access through the UT Regents' Promise Plus endowment. Promise Plus launched in 2022 as a $300 million endowment that was created by the UT System regents to reduce the cost of higher education for lower income students.[[21]](#cite_note-21) In 2024, Milliken and the regents expanded this need-based financial aid program to provide free tuition at any of UT’s nine academic institutions for in-state undergraduate students whose families have an adjusted gross income of $100,000 or less.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

Under the chancellorship of Millken at the University of Texas System, the board of regents also invested in student well-being, approving a $16.5 million investment to "expand and improve student mental health services, student safety and alcohol education resources" at UT's 13 institutions.[[23]](#cite_note-23) Milliken also prioritized workforce development at UT and oversaw the launch of the nation’s most comprehensive industry-recognized microcredential program in higher education, offering free access to more than 45 professional certificates for students, faculty, staff and alumni across all UT institutions. Main article: [Bladder cancer](/wiki/Bladder_cancer "Bladder cancer")

"Epidemiological data on alcohol drinking and bladder cancer are suggestive of no association, although findings were not always consistent. For both habits, an explanation of the moderate increase in risk observed in some investigations might be attributed to residual confounding by smoking, or to an association between alcohol, coffee, and yet unidentified risk factors for bladder cancer."[[149]](#cite_note-149)

Main article: [Cervical cancer](/wiki/Cervical_cancer "Cervical cancer")

A study concluded "that alcoholic women are at high risk for *in situ* and invasive cervical cancer" but attributed this to indirect, lifestyle-related reasons.[[150]](#cite_note-Weiderpass-150)

"DCIS patients and control subjects did not differ with respect to oral contraceptive use, hormone replacement therapy, alcohol consumption or smoking history, or breast self-examination. Associations for LCIS were similar."[[151]](#cite_note-151)

Main article: [Ependymoma](/wiki/Ependymoma "Ependymoma")

A review of the basic literature[[152]](#cite_note-152) found that consumption of beer was associated with increased risk in one study[[153]](#cite_note-153) but not in another[[154]](#cite_note-154)

See also: [Uveal melanoma](/wiki/Uveal_melanoma "Uveal melanoma")

A study found no association between alcohol and uveal melanoma.[[155]](#cite_note-pmid14566630-155)

A [systematic review](/wiki/Systematic_review "Systematic review") found evidence that light drinking may decrease the risk of nasopharyngeal carcinoma whereas high intake of alcohol may increase the risk.[[156]](#cite_note-156)

Armisen joined the cast of *[Saturday Night Live](/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live "Saturday Night Live")* in [2002](/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live_season_28 "Saturday Night Live season 28").[[42]](#cite_note-42) He was promoted to a repertory player in [2004](/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live_season_30 "Saturday Night Live season 30"). After 11 years as a cast member, he decided to leave the show. At the time of his [2013](/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live_season_38 "Saturday Night Live season 38") departure from the show,[[43]](#cite_note-splitsider-43)[[44]](#cite_note-44) Armisen was the third-longest-tenured cast member (behind [Seth Meyers](/wiki/Seth_Meyers "Seth Meyers") and [Darrell Hammond](/wiki/Darrell_Hammond "Darrell Hammond")), and he appeared in the second-highest number of sketches (856) of any cast member. Since then, Armisen has come back for multiple cameo appearances on the show, including when he hosted the season 41 finale on May 21, 2016, with musical guest [Courtney Barnett](/wiki/Courtney_Barnett "Courtney Barnett").
